passages.source_text: κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐκοῦν ὀρθῶς ἔχει τὰ ὑπὸ ποιητῶν καὶ φιλοσόφων λεγόμενα ὡς ἐν ᾅδου αἱ ψυχαὶ τῶν ἀσεβῶν κριθεῖσαι ἐφ’ οἷς ἐτόλμησαν κολάζονται, οἷον Ἰξίωνος καὶ Ταντάλου Τιτυοῦ τε καὶ Σισύφου καὶ τῶν Δαναοῦ θυγατέρων καὶ ὅσοι ποτὲ ἄλλοι ἐνταῦθα ἠσέβησαν; καὶ πῶς, εἴγε ταῦθ’ οὕτως μὴ ἔχει, δυνατὸν ἂν μαγείαν ὑφεστάναι; τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος οὕτω τὰ ἐν ᾅδου ἔχειν, ἐγὼ ἐπυθόμην Διὰ τί δὴ καὶ αὐτοὶ μαγείαν οὐ πεφοβήμεθα, ἐπὶ μοιχείας πεπεισμένοι τὴν ἐν ᾅδου δίκην; μαγείᾳ γὰρ βιάσασθαι τὴν μὴ θέλουσαν οὐ συντίθεμαι εἶναι δίκαιον. εἰ δέ τις αὐτὴν πείθειν ἐπαγγέλλεται, πρὸς τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦ καὶ χάριν ὁμολογεῖν ἑτοίμως ἔχω.

καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἔφη Οὐ δοκεῖ σοι ταὐτὸν εἶναι εἴτε μαγείᾳ αὐτῆς ἐπιτύχοις εἴτε πείσας λόγοις; κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐ πάντως ὅμοιον· πολὺ γὰρ ἀφέστηκεν ἀλλήλων ἑκάτερον· ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἄκουσαν γυναῖκα τῇ τῆς μαγείας βίᾳ ἐπαναγκάσας ὡς ἐπιβουλεύσας σώφρονι χαλεπωτάτην ὑπέχει τὴν δίκην, ὁ δὲ λόγῳ πείσας καὶ ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῆς ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ βουλῇ ποιησάμενος τὴν παράφασιν οὐκ ἐβιάσατο. ἧττον δὲ οἶμαι κολασθήσεσθαι τὸν πεπεικότα τοῦ βιασαμένου· τοιγαροῦν εἰ μὲν πεῖσαι δύνασαι, χάριν ἕξω ἐπιτυχών, ἄλλως δὲ ἥδιόν μοι τεθνάναι μᾶλλον ἢ τὴν μὴ βουλημένην βιαίως ἐπαναγκάσαι.

καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἀληθῶς διαπορῶν ἔφη Τί με χρὴ πρὸς σὲ λέγειν; ποτὲ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ὑπὸ ἔρωτος ἐνοχλούμενος εὔχῃ ἐπιτυχεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ ὡς οὐκ ἐρῶν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας προτιμᾷς τὸν φόβον. καὶ οἴει πείσας μὲν ὡς ἀναμάρτητος ἔσεσθαι ἀνεύθυνος, βίᾳ δὲ τῇ τῆς μαγείας ἐπιτυχὼν ὑφέξειν δίκην. ἀλλ’ ἀγνοεῖς ὡς τὸ τέλος παντὸς πράγματος κρίνεται ὅτι γέγονεν, οὐ τὸ πῶς γέγονεν δοκιμάζεται. καὶ σὺ δὲ ἐὰν μοιχεύσῃς οὐ δήπου μαγείᾳ μὲν δυνηθεὶς ὡς ἀσεβήσας κριθῇσῃ, πείσας δὲ τῆς κατὰ τὴν μοιχείαν ἁμαρτίας ἀπολυθήσῃ. κἀγὼ ἔφην Διὰ τὸ ἐρᾶν πάντως μοι προκειμένου τυχεῖν τῆς ἐρωμένης, ἀνάγκη μὲν μοὶ ἑλέσθαι θάτερον, αἱρήσομαι δὲ (εἰ οἷόν τε) κολακεῦσαι μᾶλλον ἢ μαγεῦσαι. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ κολακείᾳ πείθειν αὐτὴν ῥάδιον· πάνυ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ γυνὴ φιλόσοφος.

καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἔφη Ταύτῃ μᾶλλον εὔελπίς εἰμι πείσειν αὐτὴν δυνήσεσθαι ὡς αὐτὸς θέλεις, εἴπεργε προσομιλῆσαι αὐτῇ δυνάμεθα. κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Ἀδύνατον. καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἐπύθετο εἰ ἐπιστεῖλαι αὐτῇ δυνατόν ἐστιν. κἀγὼ ἔφην Δυνατὸν τοῦτό γε. καὶ ὁ Ἀππίων ἔφη Ἔτι τῇ νυκτὶ ταύτῃ συγγράψω βιβλίον, μοιχείας ἐγκώμιον, ὅπερ σὺ παρ’ ἐμοῦ λαβὼν διαπέμψεις αὐτῇ, καὶ ἐλπίζω ὅτι πεισθεῖσα συνθήσεται. καὶ συγγράψας ὁ Ἀππίων ἐκεῖνο τὸ βιβλίον ἐδίδου ἐμοί, περὶ οὗ καὶ ἐν τῇ νυκτὶ ταύτῃ ἐνενόησα καὶ εὐκαίρως ἔχειν αὐτὸ ὑπεμνήσθην σὺν ἄλλοις βιβλίοις οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι. διηγησάμενος δὲ ταῦτα ἔδειξα τοῖς παροῦσι τὸ βιβλίον, καὶ βουλομένοις ἐπακοῦσαι ἀνέγνων, καὶ δὴ ἀναγνοὺς ἔφην Αὕτη ἐστίν, ἄνδρες, ἡ τῶν Ἑλλήνων παιδεία, γενναίαν ὑπόθεσιν ἔχουσα πρὸς τὸ ἀδεῶς ἐξαμαρτάνειν. τὸ δὲ βιβλίον ἦν οὕτως ἔχον·

Ὁ ἐρῶν τῇ ἐρωμένῃ (ἀνωνύμως διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων νόμους). ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδὸς χάριν. ἔγνων σε φιλοσοφίᾳ προσανέχουσαν καὶ ἀρετῆς ἕνεκα τὸν τῶν κρεττόνων ζηλοῦσαν βίον. τίνες δὲ ἂν εἶεν κρείττονες ἢ θεοὶ μὲν ἁπάντων, ἀνθρώπων δὲ οἱ φιλόσοφοι; οὗτοι γὰρ μόνοι ἴσασιν τῶν ἔργων ποῖα μὲν ἐστὶν φύσει κακὰ ἢ καλά, ποῖα δὲ τῇ τῶν νόμων θέσει (οὐκ ὄντα) νομίζεται. αὐτίκα γοῦν τὴν λεγομένην μοιχείαν πρᾶξίν τινες ὑπειλήφασιν εἶναι κακήν, καίτοι καλὴν κατὰ πάντα ὑπάρχουσαν· εἰς γὰρ τὴν τοῦ βίου πολυγονίαν ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος γίνεται. Ἔρως δὲ ἐστὶν ὁ πάντων θεῶν πρεσβύτατος. ἄνευ γὰρ δὴ Ἔρωτος οὐ στοιχείων, οὐ θεῶν, οὐκ ἀνθρώπων, οὐ ζῴων ἀλόγων, οὐ τῶν λοιπῶν ἁπάντων μίξις ἢ γένεσις γενέσθαι δύναται. πάντες γάρ τοι ὄργανά ἐσμεν τοῦ Ἔρωτος. αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ δι’ ἡμῶν τεχνίτης, παντὸς τοῦ γεννωμένου ψυχαῖς ἐπιδημῶν, ἐστὶ νοῦς. ὅθεν οὐκ αὐτοὶ θέλοντες, ἀλλ’ ὅταν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελευσθῶμεν, τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα ποιεῖν ἐπιθυμοῦμεν. εἰ δ’ ἐκείνου βουλῇ ἐπιθυμοῦντες χάριν τῆς λεγομένης σωφροσύνης κρατεῖν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἐπιχειρήσομεν, πῶς τῷ πάντων πρεσβυτάτῳ θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἀντιπράττοντες οὐ τὰ μέγιστα ἀσεβήσομεν;

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: And I said, “Then are the things said by poets and philosophers correct: that in Hades the souls of the impious, after being judged for what they dared to do, are punished—such as the souls of Ixion, Tantalus, Tityus, Sisyphus, the daughters of Danaus, and all the others who ever acted impiously here? And if these things are not so, how could magic have any reality?” When he said that matters in Hades were indeed so, I asked, “Why, then, have we ourselves not feared magic, since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery? For I do not agree that it is right to use magic to force a woman who is unwilling. But if someone promises to persuade her, I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: how could magic have any reality
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφεστάναι has an existential sense here: magic could not subsist or be real if the premises about Hades were false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have we ourselves not feared magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first-person plural is retained as an inclusive rhetorical question; αὐτοί adds emphasis, ‘we ourselves.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μοιχείας πεπεισμένοι τὴν ἐν ᾅδου δίκην
lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπὶ μοιχείας identifies adultery as the ground for the punishment; πεπεισμένοι governs the conviction expressed by τὴν ... δίκην.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦ καὶ χάριν ὁμολογεῖν ἑτοίμως ἔχω
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑτοίμως ἔχω expresses readiness, while χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means to acknowledge gratitude or indebtedness.

passages.text: And Appion said, “Do you not think it amounts to the same thing whether you obtain her by magic or by persuading her with words?” I said, “They are not at all alike; each is far removed from the other. The man who compels an unwilling woman by magic’s force incurs the harshest punishment as one who has schemed against a chaste woman. But the man who persuades her by speech and makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice has used no force. Still, I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force. So if you can persuade her, I will be grateful if I succeed; otherwise, I would rather die than forcibly compel a woman who does not consent.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you obtain her
lexical_decisions.rationale: With a person as the genitive object in this erotic context, ἐπιτυγχάνω means to attain or succeed in obtaining that person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῆς ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ βουλῇ ποιησάμενος τὴν παράφασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: παράφασις can denote an appeal, exhortation, or persuasion. The ἐπί phrase makes her own authority and will the basis on which the appeal succeeds; the defensible alternative ‘makes the persuasion subject to her own freedom and will’ has the same contrast with force.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧττον δὲ οἶμαι κολασθήσεσθαι τὸν πεπεικότα τοῦ βιασαμένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τοῦ βιασαμένου supplies the standard of comparison after ἧττον.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will be grateful if I succeed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the speaker will ‘have gratitude’ upon succeeding; English expresses this naturally as being grateful.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would rather die than
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative wording is emphatic in Greek; idiomatic English expresses the preference with ‘rather ... than.’

passages.text: And Appion, genuinely at a loss, said, “What am I to say to you? At one moment, as a man tormented by love, you wish to obtain her; at another, as if you were not in love, you put fear before desire. You imagine that after persuading her you will be free from liability as though sinless, but that if you obtain her by the force of magic, you will incur punishment. Yet you fail to understand that what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened—not how it happened. And if you commit adultery, surely you will not be judged to have acted impiously if you manage it by magic, yet be absolved of the sin involved in adultery if you persuade her.” I said, “Because I am in love, obtaining the woman I love is in any case my settled aim. I must therefore choose one of the two, and, if possible, I will choose to flatter rather than use magic. But it is not easy to persuade her even with flattery, for the woman is thoroughly a philosopher.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: genuinely at a loss
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαπορέω conveys serious perplexity or uncertainty about how to proceed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you put fear before desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive marks the thing over which fear is preferred; ‘prefer fear to desire’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will be free from liability as though sinless
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεύθυνος means not liable or not accountable, while ὡς ἀναμάρτητος presents the supposed basis for that exemption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τέλος παντὸς πράγματος κρίνεται ὅτι γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέλος denotes the resulting end or outcome. The following ὅτι γέγονεν clarifies that the occurrence itself, rather than its manner, is in view.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if you manage it by magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle δυνηθείς leaves the action implicit; the context supplies succeeding in the adultery through magic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνυ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ γυνὴ φιλόσοφος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the woman is thoroughly a philosopher
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάνυ intensifies the predicate φιλόσοφος; ‘very much a philosopher’ is more literal but less idiomatic.

passages.text: And Appion said, “For that very reason I am more confident that I will be able to persuade her as you yourself wish, if indeed we can speak with her.” I answered, “Impossible.” Appion asked whether it was possible to write to her. I said, “That is possible.” Then Appion said, “Before this night is over, I will compose a book, an encomium to adultery. You will take it from me and send it on to her, and I hope that, once persuaded, she will consent.” Appion composed that book and gave it to me. It was about this book that I thought during this night, and at just the right time I was reminded that I had it among the other books I carry with me. After relating these things, I showed the book to those present and read it aloud when they wished to hear it. And then, after reading it, I said, “Gentlemen, this is the education of the Greeks, with a noble theme for sinning without fear.” The book ran as follows:

lexical_decisions.chosen: For that very reason I am more confident
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ταύτῃ is taken causally as referring to the woman’s being a philosopher. It could more formally be rendered ‘in this respect,’ but the causal connection is contextually stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Before this night is over
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔτι with the temporal dative indicates that the composition will occur while the present night still lasts; ‘this very night’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once persuaded, she will consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι here means to agree or consent to the proposed relationship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at just the right time I was reminded that I had it
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκαίρως is taken with the act of being reminded. A possible alternative attachment is ‘I was reminded that I conveniently had it,’ but the temporal reading is more natural in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σὺν ἄλλοις βιβλίοις οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: among the other books I carry with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative οἷς is understood by case attraction to βιβλίοις, and the reflexive phrase is interpreted contextually with the first-person verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the education of the Greeks
lexical_decisions.rationale: παιδεία may also mean Greek culture or intellectual formation; ‘education’ preserves the immediate connection with the philosophical book just read.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γενναίαν ὑπόθεσιν ἔχουσα πρὸς τὸ ἀδεῶς ἐξαμαρτάνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: with a noble theme for sinning without fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording is ironic: γενναίαν calls the book’s ὑπόθεσις ‘noble,’ while the purpose or tendency expressed by πρός is fearless wrongdoing.

source_issues.issue: The third-person reflexive ἑαυτοῦ occurs with the first-person verb ἐπιφέρομαι. Later Greek can extend ἑαυτοῦ beyond strict third-person reference, so the supplied wording remains intelligible as ‘with me’; the classically expected first-person reflexive would be ἐμαυτοῦ.

passages.text:
The Lover to His Beloved
(Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people)

At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child. I have learned that you devote yourself to philosophy and, for virtue’s sake, emulate the life of those who are superior. And who could be superior? The gods are superior to all, and philosophers to other human beings. For philosophers alone know which actions are evil or good by nature, and which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws. Take, for example, the act called adultery: some have supposed it to be evil, although it is good in every respect, for it takes place at Love’s commands for the multiplication of life. Love is the oldest of all gods. For without Love no mingling or generation can take place—of elements, of gods, of human beings, of irrational animals, or of all the remaining things. Indeed, we are all instruments of Love. But the craftsman himself, working through us and present in the souls of every being that is generated, is Mind. Consequently, it is not of our own volition that we desire to do his will, but when we are commanded by him. And if, while desiring by his will, we attempt for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire, how will we not commit the greatest acts of impiety by opposing the oldest of all gods and human beings?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: The Lover to His Beloved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative sender and dative recipient form an epistolary heading. ἐρωμένη denotes the woman loved or desired.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωνύμως διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων νόμους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ marks the foolish people as the source of the laws; ‘because of the laws made by foolish people’ is an equivalent contextual rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδὸς χάριν
lexical_decisions.chosen: At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἔρωτος naturally depends on ἐπιταγαῖς, τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου describes Love, and παιδὸς χάριν forms a separate postpositional phrase. An alternative attachment would take ‘the oldest child of all’ together, but that leaves the relation of ἐπιταγαῖς less clear and fits the subsequent description of Love as the oldest god less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνες δὲ ἂν εἶεν κρείττονες ἢ θεοὶ μὲν ἁπάντων, ἀνθρώπων δὲ οἱ φιλόσοφοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: And who could be superior? The gods are superior to all, and philosophers to other human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitives can be read comparatively: gods surpass all and philosophers surpass humans. A partitive nuance, ‘the gods among all and philosophers among humans,’ is also possible; the main rendering makes the implied comparison explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For philosophers alone know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The demonstrative most naturally resumes the immediately preceding philosophers, who possess the claimed philosophical discernment. It could grammatically encompass both gods and philosophers, but the argument is directed to the recipient’s philosophical learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποῖα δὲ τῇ τῶν νόμων θέσει (οὐκ ὄντα) νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The omitted predicate is supplied from ‘evil or good’; the parenthetical οὐκ ὄντα denies that the actions possess by nature the qualities assigned by law.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς γὰρ τὴν τοῦ βίου πολυγονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the multiplication of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολυγονία denotes abundant generation or production of offspring. ‘For life’s abundant procreation’ is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of irrational animals
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄλογος contrasts nonhuman animals as lacking reason; ‘non-rational living creatures’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: present in the souls of every being that is generated
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω literally denotes residing, sojourning, or being present among; here it describes Mind’s presence in the souls of generated beings.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is Mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοῦς is capitalized because the passage identifies it as the craftsman operating through all beings; ‘intellect’ or lowercase ‘mind’ would preserve the lexical sense but less clearly convey the personified cosmic role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελευσθῶμεν, τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα
lexical_decisions.chosen: we are commanded by him ... his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronouns immediately follow the identification of the craftsman as Mind, while the argument also closely identifies that craftsman with Love’s activity. The English preserves the masculine referent without forcing a sharper distinction between Love and Mind than the passage supplies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χάριν τῆς λεγομένης σωφροσύνης κρατεῖν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφροσύνη can mean self-control, moderation, or chastity. ‘Self-control’ suits the immediately following attempt to master sexual desire, while ‘so-called chastity’ remains a viable context-specific alternative.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
